Do not come to America. (At least, not RIGHT now.) I can’t believe I’m saying this. Normally, I’m the guy who tells you to take a chance, work hard, and figure it out. I’ve been making content about studying in the United States for almost 10 years. America has completely changed my life. But If you’ve just finished your bachelor’s degree in India and are thinking about taking a massive loan to study in the US, I want you to think twice. There are 2 reasons for this. 1. The job market. I know students applying to hundreds of jobs just to get a handful of interviews. One student applied to 1,400 jobs and got only 3 interview calls. Another took almost a year after graduation to land a software engineering role. And these are the realities you need to consider before spending tens of thousands of dollars on a degree. 2. Immigration and the political climate. There’s growing uncertainty around policies affecting international students, OPT, H-1B visas, and work authorization. Some proposed changes may never become law. But when you’re taking a massive loan to study in another country, you need to think about what happens if the rules change while you’re there. So, who should consider waiting? If you’re a fresh graduate with little work experience, no clear career direction, and a huge loan to repay, I’d seriously consider gaining 2–3 years of relevant experience in India first. Build your skills. Save money. Figure out the role you want and start preparing before you arrive. But if you have relevant work experience, a clear plan, strong preparation, or a scholarship that reduces your financial risk, your situation could be very different. The question is whether you can handle the downside if things don’t go as planned. Don’t come because your friends are coming or social media makes life in America look exciting. And don’t take a massive loan without thinking about what happens if you can’t find a job. I’m not saying you should give up on America. I’m saying you need to understand the risk before you make the decision. Come prepared, with a plan beyond simply hoping things will work out. #USA #lifeinusa
As an immigrant, I’m watching these changes closely. The US isn’t unique, since many countries are tightening their immigration policies, but it is changing its rules very fast. Nearly every week brings a smaller or bigger change. If someone goes to the US as a student right now, I would consider the possibility that staying after graduation may no longer be possible. We have OPT today, but whether it will still exist in two years is uncertain. The rules for H-1B have also become much stricter. Maybe we’ll see a rule that companies must lay off H-1B holders before any US citizens are affected. Maybe companies that do layoffs will be barred from sponsoring H-1B visas for a while. These are only ideas and may never happen, but they’re certainly possible.
Spot on, Yudi. I've been giving this same advice to people in my circle for the past year. So many people aren't thinking in terms of career or life at all and they're coming because friends or loved ones are already here, or simply because families are sending them. It's become a default path rather than a deliberate decision. This is such a needed reality check for everyone, because it's genuinely not like it used to be like before. The job market is brutal, the visa uncertainty is real, and then people end up struggling with massive loans after graduation with no clear path forward. Nobody should be coming assuming making a six-figure is true in everyone's case. Appreciate you putting this out there even though it's uncomfortable to say. Come with a plan, not just hope.
Pritesh Jagani 3w Report this post The average U.S. job search now takes over 6 months. I came across this recently, and I keep thinking about what it means for international students trying to build a career in the U.S. When I moved to America, I had to figure out the job market as I went. I started out on a software engineering path, then realized I wanted to move into product management or business analysis. I faced rejections because my profile didn’t clearly show why I was a fit for those roles. It took time, guidance, and a lot of reworking to understand how to position my experience. With a job search stretching beyond six 6 , having a plan becomes even more important. A few things I’d focus on: →Be intentional with applications. Focus on roles that align with your skills instead of applying everywhere. → Build relationships before you need them. Networking can help you understand teams, roles, and opportunities that may never make it to a job board. → Show your work. Make it easier for employers to see how you think, solve problems, and contribute. → Give yourself a longer runway. Plan your finances, keep learning, and make room for a job search that may take longer than expected. A longer search can be emotionally and financially exhausting, especially when you’re navigating immigration timelines at the same time. But a slow job search doesn’t define your ability or your future. Keep reviewing your approach, learning from each step, and adapting to what the market is telling you. If you’re currently looking for a job in the U.S., I hope you’re giving yourself the time, support, and structure to get through it. ❤️ #JobsearchUSA #jobs #hiring #USjobmarket 35 1 Comment Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

Pritesh Jagani 10mo Report this post It is definitely not easy to be a job seeker and an international student in the USA. To make it, you are expected to handle things most people never even think about: 1. Spend 30 to 60 Lakhs on education with zero guarantee of a job at the end. 2. Work twice as hard for half the certainty. 3. Compete with students who grew up here, know the culture, and already have networks. 4. Apply to hundreds of roles where your resume is filtered out because of your visa status. 5. Learn new technologies at a pace you have never experienced before just to stay relevant. 6. Build U.S. experience while being rejected for not having U.S. experience. 7. Balance coursework, projects, rent, groceries, CPT rules, and part-time shifts. 8. Prepare for interviews with the pressure of OPT and STEM OPT deadlines behind you. 9. Live far from home, often alone, while pretending everything is fine on video calls. 10. Watch friends get offers before you and still keep your confidence steady. 11. Manage constant doubt about finances, career, identity, and the future. 12. Know that one bad term, one missed opportunity, or one market shift can reset everything. Being an international student is not just hard. It is consistently demanding in a way that never fully turns off. Over the years, I’ve met hundreds of students who went through this journey. Some made it. Some also returned home. This path itself is unforgiving. Yet, despite everything, thousands choose this path every year. Because the opportunities can change not just your life, but your entire family’s future. Because one offer here can lift years of struggle back home. While this journey is difficult, it opens doors you cannot find anywhere else. As long as you know and understand the reality, it’s just a matter of if and not when things work out for you. Talent, skill, and capability are on hand, but mental strength and the right mindset are even more important. P.S: Every week, I share insights like this for international students and job seekers. Join 45,000+ readers who are turning their U.S. journey into a success story worth telling. Pritesh Jagani 8mo Report this post As an international student in the US, you will often feel like you are behind in life. You might be 24, 29, or 32. Some friends already have H1Bs. Some are buying cars and houses. Some are getting promoted while you are still trying to clear your first job search or visa step. It was simple back home. Score well in exams, and everyone knows you are doing fine. Here, it feels like there is a new scoreboard every week. LinkedIn, Instagram, and WhatsApp groups. Always someone posting a bigger salary, a better company, a faster visa, a nicer apartment. Slowly, two things happen. You feel smaller, and you start seeing people as competition instead of community. That is where many people go wrong. They stop sharing job links. They hide how they got referrals. They gatekeep lawyers, tax tips, and visa updates. They start resenting the friend who got lucky in the lottery or landed a big offer. But… Jealousy will not change your status. Gatekeeping will not bring you one extra interview. Bitterness will not pay your rent or build your credit score. But your actions will always say everything about you. Their actions will always say everything about them. So choose your side carefully. Choose to: – Share information about visa rules and deadlines when you learn something useful – Help your friends review their resumes before big applications – Tell people which tax tools, credit card tips and budgeting tricks are actually working for you – Celebrate their wins even when your own life feels slow – Build deep relationships instead of sitting alone with Google and anxiety Because staying in the US is not just about one job offer or one lottery result. It is about: – Knowing your immigration timelines and planning early – Building a basic personal finance system so you are not one paycheck away from panic – Having friends who would show up if your visa, health, or job went wrong – Becoming the kind of person others want to refer to, vouch for, and live with Kindness is not weakness. In this country, it is a long-term strategy. I still hang out with my ex-boss from my Chico days. We play poker, we chat, we hang out, and it’s been over 10 years, one of the best relationships I’ve cultivated in life. Think big. Don’t let jealousy narrow your vision. 159 11 Comments Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

Pritesh Jagani 1w Report this post Why I bought $350K home instead of the $600K home? (Though bank approved it) Because I wanted to build wealth without putting myself under years of financial pressure. Just because a bank approves you for a $600K mortgage doesn't mean you should borrow that much. 5 things I considered before buying: 1. I wanted my housing costs to stay manageable. I kept my housing costs around 20–25% of my income. That left me with room to save, invest, and handle unexpected expenses instead of stretching my finances to afford a bigger house. 2. The mortgage wasn't the WHOLE cost. Owning a home meant paying for more than just the monthly mortgage. I also had to account for: - Property taxes - Homeowners insurance - HOA fees - Repairs and maintenance These costs can add up quickly, even when the mortgage payment seems affordable. 3. What if I suddenly lost my job? As an H-1B holder, losing my job could affect more than my paycheck. It could also create uncertainty around my immigration status. I wanted ONE FULL YEAR of housing costs saved in a HYSA. That way, I'd have accessible savings to cover my housing expenses if I suddenly lost my income. 4. How long was I planning to stay in America? Buying a home comes with upfront and selling costs. If I sold too soon, closing costs and realtor fees could eat into my money. I had to think about whether I planned to stay in America long enough for buying to make financial sense. 5. I wanted to KEEP my options open. Buying a home can help you build equity, but it also ties up your money and can make relocating more complicated. For immigrants, career and immigration plans can change. Renting can sometimes offer the FLEXIBILITY to move when circumstances change. This is what I have learned: Renting isn't automatically throwing money away. And buying a home doesn't automatically mean you're building wealth. The right decision depends on your finances, your plans, and how much flexibility you want to keep. #FinanceUSA #HomeUSA 58 2 Comments Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

Rakshit Goyal 12mo Report this post As soon as I landed in the U.S as an international student, I knew that if I was going to build a life and a career here, I had to build a network. Without wasting any time, I scheduled time with my program director, my dean, my professors, and reached out to my classmates from every major before I even started classes. I was an international student carrying the weight of student loans, cultural shock, and survival pressure. So I set one small, intentional goal: Meet one new person every day for the first few weeks. Then, eventually, one new professional connection every week. I started with university clubs, events, volunteer opportunities, and anything that offered a face-to-face connection. Even when my budget was tight, I learned to invest in people because I knew a $4 coffee could open more doors than a $400 course. Here’s what intentional networking did for me and can do for you: 1. Start early, start small. You don’t need a perfect elevator pitch. You need curiosity and consistency. 2. It’s not about asking for a job. It’s about building trust, sharing stories, learning how people think and work before you ever need a favor. 3. Networking is long-term career insurance. Roles change, companies restructure, visas expire, but strong relationships keep doors open. 4. Not all connections are created equal. Some people will become mentors. Others may just offer one key piece of advice. Every conversation matters. Energy is a currency. Invest it wisely. Focus on communities and people who energize, not drain you. If you’re a student, job seeker, or recent immigrant, I know it’s overwhelming. But networking isn’t just for extroverts or executives. It’s for anyone building a future from scratch. So many meaningful opportunities in my career came from a relationship. So if you’re reading this and feel unsure where to start, today’s goal is simple: - - Send a message. - - Schedule that coffee. - - Show up at that event, even if you feel awkward. You never know what (or who) it might lead to. P.S. I'm Rakshit .
